ogTitle: 10 Most Popular Attractions in Tak 2026 — Thi Lo Su, Bhumibol Dam, Old Town
ogDesc: Thi Lo Su Waterfall in Umphang, Bhumibol Dam, the King Taksin Shrine, Wat Thai Watthanaram in Mae Sot, Trok Ban Chin, the Kad Nang Yong walking street, Doi Musoe — the 10 Tak attractions real visitors talk about, with entry fees and locations.
eyebrow: See it like a Tak local · Updated 2026
intro: Tak is the province that packs every kind of trip into one place — from Thi Lo Su, one of Thailand's biggest waterfalls, deep in the pristine jungle of Umphang, to Bhumibol Dam on its vast reservoir, to the old town on the Ping River and the Tai Yai temples of Mae Sot. Here are the 10 attractions real visitors talk about most, with entry fees, locations, and trip-planning tips — whether you're covering Tak town in a day or pushing deep into Umphang for an overnight adventure.

blocks.html:
Tak's charm is that one province feels like several different worlds. In Tak town along the Ping River there's the old quarter of Trok Ban Chin, where the wooden houses of Chinese merchants still line the alley for a vintage photo walk; the white Rattanakosin Bicentennial suspension bridge that lights up beautifully at night; and Kad Nang Yong Khlong Yam, the walking street where you squat down to browse goods laid out on low bamboo platforms. Drive up the mountain toward Mae Sot and you reach Doi Musoe Market with its cool-climate fruit and vegetables. Nature lovers get Lan Sang National Park near town, Bhumibol Dam at Sam Ngao, and — at the far end — Thi Lo Su, deep in the Umphang jungle, reached by truck, rubber raft, and a jungle hike. Shrines, old town, nature, cafés — all in one province.

This list includes the pins no Tak trip should skip: Thi Lo Su Waterfall, a limestone cascade roughly 500 meters wide and 300 meters tall that ranks among the largest and most beautiful in Thailand; Bhumibol Dam, the country's largest and tallest arch concrete dam; the King Taksin the Great Shrine, enshrining the royal statue seated on the throne with a sword laid across his lap — where Tak locals come to pray for power and authority; and Wat Thai Watthanaram in Mae Sot, a Tai Yai temple in Burmese style with a golden wihan against deep-red walls and a giant reclining Buddha that has become a favorite photo spot. Scroll on for the details of each stop and build your own route.

blocks.name: Thi Lo Su Waterfall
blocks.signature: Huge limestone waterfall roughly 500 m wide and 300 m tall, cascading in tiers through pristine jungle — regarded as one of Thailand's largest and most beautiful waterfalls; reached by truck, rubber raft, and a jungle hike
blocks.priceRange: Sanctuary entry ~฿20 + truck-raft-guide fees per package
blocks.descHtml:
If you're going to pick one waterfall to see once in your life, Thi Lo Su in the Umphang Wildlife Sanctuary is the name nature lovers agree on most. It's a huge limestone waterfall with a cliff face roughly 400–500 meters wide, cascading down in tiers over a drop of about 200–250 meters, set deep in the pristine jungle of Umphang. It's regarded as one of the largest and most beautiful waterfalls in Thailand — best suited to people who love trekking and travel that comes home with a story, rather than a park-snap-and-go waterfall.

The highlight is the sheet of white water spreading across a cliff face too wide to fit in a single frame. Review after review agrees that photos capture less than half of the real thing. The must-do is the rubber-raft float down the Mae Klong River before the hike in to the falls — the stretch many say is the most fun and the fullest immersion in the forest. And if you're lucky with the sun, you'll catch a rainbow arcing across the curtain of water — one reason Thi Lo Su is counted among Thailand's natural highlights.

On budget: the sanctuary entry fee itself is cheap — just tens of baht — but the real cost lies in the high-clearance truck or local transport, the rafting, and the guide, which most people bundle into a 2–3 day tour package from Umphang town, since the access road is a dirt track that needs a four-wheel drive. The location is genuinely remote: from Umphang it's another few dozen kilometers by vehicle plus a stretch of hiking, so allow a full day or an overnight stay.

The key thing to know is that the waterfall is seasonal — generally open from around early September through about May, with the waterfall trail closed during the rainy season (roughly Jun–Aug) for safety and forest recovery. The falls are at their most spectacular when water is high after the rains. Check opening dates and book ahead with operators in Umphang, bring trekking shoes and leech protection, and come physically ready — the charm of Thi Lo Su is earning a view that pays back every step.
mustOrder: Stand before the limestone cascade spreading across the entire cliff face in tiers
Raft the Mae Klong River before hiking in to the falls
Watch for the rainbow arcing across the falls when the sun breaks through
Swim in the clear, cool pools beneath the falls deep in the jungle
blocks.bestFor: Trekkers and adventure travelers out to conquer Thailand's biggest waterfall once in a lifetime (2–3 day trip)
blocks.hours: Tourist season ~Sep 1–May (waterfall trail closed in rainy season Jun–Aug)

blocks.name: Bhumibol Dam
blocks.signature: Thailand's largest and tallest arch concrete dam — mountain views mirrored on a vast reservoir, boat and raft cruises, floating raft stays, crest viewpoints, and a waterside café; an easy family day out
blocks.descHtml:
Bhumibol Dam (formerly Yanhee Dam) in Sam Ngao District, Tak, is the largest and tallest arch concrete dam in Thailand, holding back the Ping River at 154 meters from base to crest. If you love quiet views of green mountains mirrored on a wide sheet of water, this is your place — a family destination you can enjoy all day without rushing. Drive up onto the dam crest, stroll in the breeze, and look down over the reservoir on one side and the power plant on the other. Visitors consistently describe it as a dam with a great atmosphere and neatly kept gardens.

The highlight many people love is the raft or boat cruise into the reservoir — calling at Ko Valentine and Phra Phutthabat Khao Nam, and running as far as Kaeng Soi and Doi Tao. Some operators offer overnight floating raft stays out on the water. Real reviews mention feeding the fish along the dam crest and watching huge giant catfish gather — good fun. For a slower pace, sit at the café by the crest pavilion; the on-site restaurants get praise for good food and views, and the late-afternoon light is lovely for photos.

On budget: the dam itself is free to visit, with no entry fee and friendly, attentive security staff — you pay only for the extras you choose. Raft cruises start at around 600 baht per person for a day trip, and EGAT accommodation ranges from a few hundred baht up to group lodges in the thousands. Book ahead — long weekends fill fast.

The dam sits about 60 kilometers from Tak town and is open through the daytime. Late morning to evening is the best window for good light. It's popular because it's the province's landmark, combining historical significance, natural scenery, and water activities in one place. Worth knowing: the road up to the crest is fairly high and steep — take it slow — and raft cruises should be arranged with the operators in advance.
mustOrder: Walk the dam crest for views over the reservoir and power plant
Raft or boat cruise to Ko Valentine and Kaeng Soi
Feed the fish by the dam crest — spot the huge giant catfish
Sit at the waterside café by the crest pavilion
blocks.bestFor: Family nature outing — dam-crest views in the late afternoon

blocks.name: King Taksin the Great Shrine
blocks.area: 205 Charot Withi Thong Road, Nong Luang, Mueang Tak District, Tak
blocks.signature: Four-gabled pavilion hung with red Chinese lanterns, enshrining a statue of King Taksin seated on the throne with a sword laid across his lap, surrounded by war-horse and war-elephant figures left as offerings — the place to pray for power and authority
blocks.priceRange: Free (flower-incense-candle sets, horses, and swords available for offerings)
blocks.descHtml:
Ask a local where to pay respects first in Tak, and almost everyone will point you to the King Taksin the Great Shrine on Taksin Road near the provincial hall. This is the city's guardian shrine, part of Tak life for over 70 years — built in 1947 to a design by the Fine Arts Department. It suits worshippers praying for power, authority, and career fortune, as well as anyone collecting the city's key historical landmarks.

The highlight is the four-gabled pavilion ringed with red Chinese lanterns. Inside sits a cast statue of King Taksin, slightly larger than life, seated on the throne with his sword laid across his lap — commanding and dignified. Around the statue stand war-horse and war-elephant figures brought as votive offerings to honor his power, and in some corners fighting cocks, from the belief that the King laid down the rules of cockfighting. The inner walls carry murals telling the story of his campaign to reclaim the capital — worth a slow walk around.

On atmosphere: most reviews agree the shrine sits on a low rise opposite Taksin Rachanusorn School — shaded and pleasant to walk, with a 12-zodiac garden for photos and a spacious parking lot. Entry is free; flower-incense-candle sets with votive horses and swords are sold at the front. Light your incense outside, then bring your offering in. Come in the late afternoon and you'll get views of King Taksin Bridge against a lovely mountain backdrop.

A few things to know: this is a sacred shrine where people genuinely come to worship — dress modestly and be composed. Open daily roughly 06:00–17:30. From New Year's Eve into the new year there's an annual celebration fair, with big crowds and stalls all around the shrine — to avoid the crush, come on a weekday morning. Its Google rating runs as high as 4.8 from nearly two thousand reviewers, confirming it as one of Tak's top pins.
mustOrder: The statue of King Taksin seated on the throne, sword across his lap, in the four-gabled pavilion
Pray for power and authority, then offer war-horse and war-elephant figures
Red Chinese lanterns around the pavilion + murals of the reclaiming of the capital
The 12-zodiac garden and King Taksin Bridge views at dusk
blocks.bestFor: Praying for power and authority + the guardian landmark no Tak trip should skip
blocks.zone: Mueang Tak (Taksin Rd, near the provincial hall)

blocks.name: Wat Thai Watthanaram
blocks.area: Tha Sai Luat, Mae Sot District, Tak
blocks.signature: Tai Yai temple in Burmese style — golden wihan and chedi with gilded patterns on deep-red walls, plus a giant reclining Buddha that is Mae Sot's most popular photo and worship spot
blocks.descHtml:
Wat Thai Watthanaram — known to Mae Sot locals as "Wat Mae Tao Ngiao" or simply the "Tai Yai temple" — is one of the most beautiful Tai Yai/Burmese-style temples in Mae Sot District, about 5 kilometers from town toward the Thai–Myanmar Friendship Bridge. The wihan and chedi glow gold, with gilded patterns worked onto deep-red walls; from a distance the whole structure looks like solid gold. If you want Burmese-style temple photos without crossing the border, this delivers — a natural fit for temple-goers, architecture lovers, and anyone who enjoys a quiet walk in a border-town atmosphere.

The highlight many come specifically for is the reclining Buddha, roughly 40 meters long, enshrined in an open wihan at the back of the temple — the most popular photo and worship spot, and one several reviewers rank among the largest reclining Buddhas in Thailand. Also not to miss: the replica of the Maha Muni Buddha, modeled on the revered original in Mandalay, Myanmar, which locals hold in deep faith, plus the golden nine-spired Mon-style chedi and the pair of swan statues at the temple entrance. The wihan, the museum, and the stucco detailing make for an easy, absorbing wander.

Entry is free, with convenient parking, open daily roughly 07:00–17:00. The prettiest light comes early morning or late afternoon, when the sun isn't harsh — at midday the gold reflects so brightly that one foreign reviewer joked you should pack sunglasses. The temple ranks among Mae Sot's top attractions on international review sites, with solid scores praising the intricacy of the artistry and the calm.

Worth knowing: this is an active temple in daily religious use. Dress modestly, remove shoes before entering the wihan, and keep voices low when photographing. If it's your first day in Mae Sot, start here — Rim Moei Market and the Friendship Bridge follow on the same route.
mustOrder: The giant reclining Buddha, roughly 40 meters long
The Maha Muni replica from Mandalay
The golden nine-spired Mon-style chedi
The pair of golden swans at the temple entrance
blocks.bestFor: First stop on your first day in Mae Sot — for worshippers and Burmese-temple photographers
blocks.zone: Tha Sai Luat (near the Friendship Bridge)

blocks.name: Trok Ban Chin
blocks.area: Taksin Road, Rahaeng, Mueang Tak District, Tak
blocks.signature: Century-old Chinese community — dozens of immigrant merchants' wooden houses in a row, with cafés and food shops in the old houses; a vintage photo walk in the old quarter by the Ping River
blocks.descHtml:
If you're in Tak town and want a slow walk through the old quarter by the Ping River, Trok Ban Chin is the pin locals will point you to. It's a Chinese immigrant community over a century old, on Taksin Road in Rahaeng Subdistrict, near Wat Sitalaram and the Rattanakosin Bicentennial Bridge. In the early Rattanakosin era this was a bustling trading quarter beside the Ping River pier, moving goods between Nakhon Sawan, the North, and Burma. It suits old-town lovers, vintage-photo hunters, and anyone who enjoys quiet, uncrowded architecture walks.

The highlight is the dozens of old teak houses lining the narrow lane for about 500 meters, blending central-Thai and northern styles with Chinese and Rama V-era European classical touches. Standouts reviewers mention include Ban Chin Thong Yu, filled with antiques like a community museum; the blue Western-style house; and the Sophanodon family house with its rare double front staircase. Another must is the Pad Thai Trok Ban Chin shop — old-style pad thai served in a long-running aged wooden house, with soft thin noodles and a mellow, rounded flavor at 20–25 baht a plate — the perfect walking snack.

The mood today is quiet, a far cry from its bustling past — and that's exactly the charm. Photo walks are easy; the lane isn't long, and 15–30 minutes covers it. The best light comes before 10 AM or from about 4:30 PM onward, when it rakes across the wooden houses for that aged feel. Entry is free — you pay only at the neighborhood's food shops and cafés.

Worth knowing: the lane is very narrow — cars can't pass each other, so find parking near the entrance and walk in. And this is a living neighborhood, so walk and photograph with respect for the residents. It's popular precisely because it's a genuine riverside old town that has kept the real thing intact rather than being staged for tourism — pair it with the King Taksin Shrine and the riverside walking street in a single trip.
mustOrder: Century-old teak houses lining the lane
Ban Chin Thong Yu, an antique-filled house like a community museum
Pad Thai Trok Ban Chin — old-style pad thai in an aged wooden house
Vintage photos in the slanted morning/evening light
blocks.bestFor: Old-town lovers and vintage photo walks by the Ping — come morning or late afternoon for the best light
blocks.zone: Old town by the Ping (Taksin Rd, Rahaeng)
blocks.hours: Walkable every day (shops in the quarter roughly 08:00–17:00)
blocks.libCredit: Illustrative image: Rlevse / Wikimedia Commons (Public Domain)

blocks.title: 🛏️ Where to stay in Tak — sleep in the old town by the Ping or overnight in Umphang
blocks.text: To get the most out of Tak, stay a night — you can stroll the old riverside quarter in the evening and visit the King Taksin Shrine early in the morning while it's still quiet. The most popular stays cluster in Tak town along the Ping River, within easy walking distance of Trok Ban Chin, the Bicentennial Bridge, and the Kad Nang Yong market, with everything from small hotels in old houses to riverside stays. Heading to Mae Sot? Pick a hotel in central Mae Sot near the Friendship Bridge. And if Thi Lo Su is the mission, spend a night in Umphang — it's far away and the mountain road winds hard. Choose a location near your first morning's stop for the best value, and compare prices and reviews before booking.

blocks.name: Kad Nang Yong Khlong Yam Walking Street
blocks.signature: Riverside walking street where vendors set goods on knee-high bamboo platforms — you squat down to browse; local food and crafts, open Sat–Sun evenings roughly 16:00–21:00
blocks.descHtml:
If you're in Tak on a weekend and want small-town atmosphere unlike any other walking street, Kad Nang Yong Khlong Yam is the stop. Its signature quirk — the thing visitors remember — is that vendors set their goods on knee-high bamboo platforms, so browsing means bending or squatting down to look. The "khlong yam" part comes from Tak's multi-ethnic heritage: locals traditionally carry a yam (a woven shoulder bag), and the market invites visitors to sling one on and shop with it instead of plastic bags. It's a small charm that sets the place apart, well suited to easy strolling, local-food grazing, and anyone hunting unusual photos.

The food leans local — Tak and northern dishes, savory and sweet, to graze on as you wander — plus souvenirs, keepsakes, clothing, community handicrafts, and locally woven yam bags. Visitors describe the mood as chill: the market sits right on the Ping River, so once you're done shopping you can sit by the water, listen to the river, and catch live music playing in stretches. Sunset is the prettiest hour of all.

The market runs Saturday and Sunday evenings only, roughly 16:00–21:00. Entry is free, and a grazing budget of a few hundred baht fills you up. It's in Tak town on the Ping riverside, around the Tak Vintage Market in front of the municipal office (its more recent location after moving from the front of the old governor's residence), not far from the King Taksin the Great Shrine, with a parking area laid on — easy to reach.

Worth knowing: it opens only on weekends — come on a weekday and you'll miss it — and the site has moved before, so check the market's Facebook page before setting out in case hours or location shift with the season. Early evening is the busiest and liveliest window; if you want bamboo-platform shots with the river view, arrive before dark.
mustOrder: Squat down to browse goods on the knee-high bamboo platforms
Tak and northern local food, like khao soi and nam phrik num
Locally woven yam shoulder bags (carry one instead of a plastic bag)
Live music and Ping River views at dusk

blocks.name: Rattanakosin Bicentennial Bridge
blocks.signature: White suspension bridge over the Ping River — the prettiest river viewpoint in town, lit up at night; walk, cycle, and photograph, with a small walking street and riverside restaurants in the evening
blocks.descHtml:
If you want the prettiest Ping River viewpoint in Tak town, the Rattanakosin Bicentennial Bridge — or simply "the suspension bridge" to locals — is the answer. It's a white suspension bridge stretching across the Ping in the heart of town, built in 1982 to celebrate Bangkok's 200th anniversary as the capital. The span runs several hundred meters; the deck was originally wood held by thick steel cables, and today it's reserved for strolling and sightseeing only — no vehicles. It suits photographers, couples on an evening walk, families with kids running along the riverside, and plenty of cyclists too.

The can't-miss window is sunset into night. In the evening, orange light spills across the Ping — a scene many say stops them mid-walk to shoot — and after dark the bridge lights come on along its full length, tracing a white arc across the water that has become the town's favorite check-in. Multiple firsthand reviews agree the lights run from around 6 PM to 9 PM; come in that window for the full display.

Budget-wise it couldn't be easier: walking the bridge is free, with no entry fee. Around it, the royal commemorative park offers a public space to sit, rest, and exercise, and from evening onward riverside food stalls open into a small walking street, so a snack is never far away. It's in Pa Mamuang Subdistrict, Mueang Tak, across the river — just minutes from the town center.

A little worth knowing: it's an old suspension bridge, so a slight sway underfoot is natural for the type — no cause for alarm; walk slowly and keep a hand on the rail and you're fine. Keep an eye on small children and elderly companions. Midday sun is strong and hot, so a late-afternoon-to-evening visit gets you cool air, the views, and the lights all in one trip.
mustOrder: Walk the suspension bridge across the Ping River
Watch the sunset
Photograph the night illumination
Browse the evening walking street and riverside restaurants
blocks.bestFor: River views and photos from late afternoon into the evening
blocks.hours: Open every day around the clock (lights on roughly 18:00–21:00)

blocks.name: Doi Musoe Market
blocks.area: Doi Musoe, Highway 105 (Tak–Mae Sot), Mae Sot District, Tak
blocks.signature: Hill-tribe roadside market on the climb up the mountain — cool-climate vegetables and fruit, strawberries, avocados, and seasonal farm and forest produce; the classic souvenir stop between Tak and Mae Sot
blocks.descHtml:
Doi Musoe Market is the hill-tribe roadside market that almost everyone driving the Tak–Mae Sot route (Highway 105) stops at — it sits right where the road climbs the mountain, the air turns cool, and stalls of cool-climate vegetables and fruit line the roadside. If you're after a mid-route supply stop with produce fresh from the farm, this is the place. There are now both an old market and a new market about a kilometer apart — you can stop at both — and the new market area also has a hill-tribe museum displaying artifacts of the Musoe (Lahu) people.

The must-buys are seasonal fruit. In the cool season (roughly Jan–Feb) strawberries arrive in force — reviewers call them "big and sweet," with graded berries around 200 baht/kg and mixed sizes starting at about 120 baht/kg. Avocados are the other signature, alongside passion fruit, Asian pears, broccoli, chayote, carrots, and seasonal forest produce; the rainy season adds peaches and cherries. It's genuinely fresh from the farm — reviewers say you walk away loaded up for just a few hundred baht and it's well worth it.

The setting is a roadside market up on the mountain, with many vendors dressed in tribal clothing and coffee-and-snack shops for a rest after shopping. Free entry, parking available, open daily roughly 8:00–19:00 (some sources say it starts earlier). Tip: come in the morning for the freshest and fullest selection, just brought down from the farms; toward evening vendors often discount to close out — good prices if size doesn't matter to you.

It's popular as the natural break point on the Tak–Mae Sot run: fresh goods, fair prices, and a genuine hill-tribe atmosphere. Worth knowing: prices and produce change with the seasons — if strawberries are the goal, make sure you're coming in the cool season, and bring a cooler bag if you're carrying goods a long way home.
mustOrder: Cool-climate strawberries (cool season, Jan–Feb)
The signature avocados
Highland vegetables, passion fruit, Asian pears, seasonal forest produce
Hill-tribe processed goods and souvenirs
blocks.bestFor: Souvenir and fruit stop between Tak and Mae Sot — cool-climate fruit lovers

blocks.name: Lan Sang National Park (Lan Sang Waterfall)
blocks.area: Mae Tho, Mueang Tak District, Tak (on the Tak–Mae Sot highway)
blocks.signature: The national park closest to Tak town — the multi-tiered Lan Sang Waterfall with a standout ~40 m drop, swimming pools, and short shaded forest trails; perfect for a day trip
blocks.priceRange: Thai adults 40 baht, children 20 baht, cars 30 baht (higher for foreign visitors)
blocks.descHtml:
If you're in Tak town and craving nature without a long drive, Lan Sang National Park is the answer locals keep passing along — the park closest to town, just about 20 kilometers out along the Tak–Mae Sot road. It suits families, couples, and first-time hikers who want pretty waterfalls and shaded forest on an easy day trip, no overnight required.

The highlight not to miss is Lan Sang Waterfall itself: the standout tier drops about 40 meters, sliding out of a rock cleft in three steps into the pool below — clear, cool water with pools you can swim in to beat the heat. Before this tier you pass Lan Liang Ma Waterfall near the visitor center, the easiest to reach on foot; with more energy, Pha Phueng, Pha Noi, and Pha Thae falls continue on up the stream. The lower trail is a short walk through bamboo groves and big trees — shaded and easy going.

Most firsthand reviews praise the clean, cool water, the shaded grounds full of big trees, clean restrooms, cheap entry, and thinner crowds than the famous parks — which makes wandering pleasant. Some note the climb to the upper falls is fairly tiring and the trail may close in certain seasons. Water is fullest and prettiest from the rainy season into early winter; in the dry season the flow can drop.

On fees and hours: the park is open roughly 08:30–16:30 daily; entry is 40 baht for Thai adults, 20 baht for children, and 30 baht per car (foreign visitors pay a higher rate). There's a restaurant, coffee shop, campground, and lodging you can book overnight. Its Google rating sits around 4.0 from several hundred reviewers — proof of a near-town escape that Tak locals and Mae Sot-route regulars visit steadily. Worth knowing: it's a natural area — bring comfortable walking shoes and a change of clothes if you'll swim, and carry your trash out, as the park keeps no bins in order to stay clean.
mustOrder: Lan Sang Waterfall — the standout ~40 m three-step tier with a swimming pool
Lan Liang Ma Waterfall by the visitor center, the easiest walk
The shaded nature trail through the bamboo groves
Camp overnight for the cool park air
blocks.bestFor: Nature lovers after a waterfall swim — an easy day trip from Tak town

blocks.name: Thiang Na Coffee and Bakery Farm
blocks.signature: Garden café-bakery in a converted wooden house — natural-style garden and air-conditioned zones, pet friendly, QR ordering at the table; known for its bread, cakes, and coffee, and a favorite photo stop in Tak
blocks.descHtml:
If you're driving through Tak on Phahonyothin Road and want a break, Thiang Na Coffee and Bakery Farm is the stop that Tak locals and northbound travelers treat as a regular. It's a garden café-bakery in a vintage wooden house converted into cozy corners, with both a shaded garden zone under big trees and a cool air-conditioned room. Traveling with a pet? Bring it along — the place is pet friendly. The mood suits a long, unhurried coffee just as well as a quick photo stop en route.

The signature that reviews agree on is the bakery — above all the croissants, soft-crumbed and buttery with several fillings to choose from, plus cakes, cookies, brioche, and scones. The coffee comes in light, medium, and dark roasts, with specialty beans from several brands available as drip. Savory dishes span Thai, Italian, and Japanese menus, all ordered easily by QR code at the table — no queueing required, ideal for anyone who wants to stay settled in their seat.

On budget: pastries run roughly 60–200 baht apiece depending on the item, with coffee and drinks at typical café prices. Entry is free — you pay only for what you order. The shop is at 27/28 Phahonyothin Road, Mai Ngam, Mueang Tak, open daily 08:00–18:00, right on the main road with easy parking — perfect as a first stop or a rest point before moving on.

It's popular because it checks every box: a photogenic garden setting, well-made bakery, and a history long enough to make it Tak's landmark café. Worth knowing: on long weekends it gets crowded and the popular pastries sell out fast — if you're set on a favorite croissant filling, come in the morning or call ahead to reserve.
mustOrder: Croissants in several fillings
Fresh-baked cakes and pastries
Drip coffee with specialty beans
The garden and waterside photo corners
blocks.bestFor: Photo-and-coffee stop on the drive north

blocks.title: 🎫 Tickets, tours, and activities in Tak
blocks.text: Want to hit several Tak spots without planning it all yourself — or without organizing the Umphang jungle on your own? Browse tickets and guided tours with transfers on Klook or GetYourGuide: complete Thi Lo Su packages covering the truck ride, rubber raft, and jungle hike, Bhumibol Dam boat trips, and airport transfer packages you can book in advance — no queueing on arrival. Ideal for easy, comfortable travel, especially the Umphang trip, where a guide leads you into the jungle and lodging and meals are arranged for you.

blocks.title: What to know before you visit Tak

items.title: Driving yourself or renting a car works best
items.text: Tak town's sights are walkable between each other, but Bhumibol Dam, Doi Musoe, Mae Sot, and Umphang lie outside town in different directions and far apart, and public transport is limited. The most practical approach is renting a car or booking tours with transfers. Grab barely exists in Tak — sort out your transport before leaving town.

items.title: Carry cash
items.text: Temples, shrines, food at the Kad Nang Yong market, Doi Musoe Market, and most shops in Trok Ban Chin run on cash. Keep small notes for entry fees, parking, roadside snacks, and shrine offerings. ATMs are easy to find in town but scarce at out-of-town sights and in Umphang.

items.title: Mornings and evenings are the best time in town
items.text: Midday in Tak is hot and glaring. The King Taksin Shrine and Trok Ban Chin are more comfortable in the morning or late afternoon; the Bicentennial Bridge is prettiest in the evening when the lights come on; and the Kad Nang Yong Khlong Yam market runs only on Saturday and Sunday evenings — plan your days to match if the walking street is on your list.

items.title: Thi Lo Su takes advance planning
items.text: Thi Lo Su Waterfall sits deep in the Umphang jungle, reached by truck, rubber raft, and a hike. Going independently is hard and requires wildlife-sanctuary permission — the easiest route is a tour package that covers vehicle, raft, guide, and lodging. The best window for water and easy access is after the rainy season, roughly November to April.

items.title: Dress modestly at temples and shrines
items.text: The King Taksin Shrine and Wat Thai Watthanaram are sacred places of active worship. Cover shoulders and knees, remove shoes where signed, and keep voices low inside the wihan.

items.title: English is limited
items.text: Outside the major sights, English signs and menus are scarce. Carry a translation app, or simply point at pictures in markets and local restaurants — it works. Most Tak locals are kind and patient with travelers.

blocks.title: Plan your Tak trip to get the most out of it
blocks.html:
Tak covers many styles of travel, but the good stuff sits in different zones, so split your trip clearly. For a half-day to one-day loop of Tak town, start at the King Taksin the Great Shrine on Taksin Road in the morning, then walk on to Trok Ban Chin in the old riverside quarter nearby, before crossing to the Rattanakosin Bicentennial Bridge in the evening when the lights come on. If it's a weekend, don't miss the Kad Nang Yong Khlong Yam market on the Ping riverside from roughly 4 PM to 9 PM. A café like Thiang Na Coffee and Bakery Farm at Mai Ngam makes an easy mid-day garden break.

Nature splits into two directions. Toward Sam Ngao is Bhumibol Dam, with boat cruises past mountains mirrored on the water. Along the Tak–Mae Sot road are Lan Sang National Park — the closest to town, good for a waterfall swim on a day trip — and Doi Musoe Market, the cool-climate fruit stop en route. Continuing to Mae Sot, stop to pay respects at Wat Thai Watthanaram near the Friendship Bridge. Thi Lo Su in Umphang is the deepest push — truck, rubber raft, then a hike — so set aside an overnight and book a tour package in advance: the distance from town is long and the mountain road winds hard.

blocks.text: To get the most from Tak, stay a night — evening strolls in the old quarter by the Ping and an early, quiet morning visit to the King Taksin Shrine. And if you're pushing into Umphang for Thi Lo Su, an overnight is required anyway. Compare Tak hotel prices and reviews before you book.

faq.q: Which Tak attractions should I not miss?
faq.a: The pins visitors rarely skip: Thi Lo Su Waterfall in Umphang, a huge limestone waterfall deep in pristine jungle regarded as one of the largest and most beautiful in Thailand; Bhumibol Dam in Sam Ngao, the country's largest and tallest arch concrete dam; the King Taksin the Great Shrine in central Tak, deeply revered and visited for blessings of power and authority; Wat Thai Watthanaram, the Burmese-style Tai Yai temple in Mae Sot; and Trok Ban Chin, the old Chinese quarter by the Ping River.

Tak's highlight is grand nature paired with a charming old town. Thi Lo Su Waterfall spreads roughly 500 meters wide and 300 meters tall, cascading through the Umphang jungle; Bhumibol Dam — Thailand's largest and tallest — mirrors the mountains on its wide reservoir. In town, Trok Ban Chin lines up the old wooden houses of Chinese merchants, the white suspension bridge across the Ping lights up at night, and the King Taksin Shrine enshrines the royal statue seated on the throne with a sword laid across his lap.

faq.q: Are Tak's attractions expensive to enter?
faq.a: Mostly free or just tens of baht. The King Taksin Shrine, Wat Thai Watthanaram, Trok Ban Chin, and the Rattanakosin Bicentennial Bridge are free. Kad Nang Yong and Doi Musoe Market are free to enter — you pay only for what you buy. Bhumibol Dam is free to visit (raft cruises from around 600 baht). Lan Sang National Park charges Thai adults 40 baht, children 20 baht, and cars 30 baht (foreigners pay more). Thi Lo Su charges a wildlife-sanctuary entry of around 20 baht plus vehicle-raft-guide costs per tour package.

faq.q: How do I get around Tak, and is parking easy?
faq.a: Tak has intercity buses from Bangkok, and Mae Sot's airport has domestic flights — but once you arrive, driving yourself or renting a car is by far the most practical option, since the sights sit in different districts and public transport is limited. In-town spots like the King Taksin Shrine, Trok Ban Chin, and the Bicentennial Bridge cluster near the Ping — park once and walk. Bhumibol Dam, Lan Sang National Park, Doi Musoe Market, and Wat Thai Watthanaram in Mae Sot each have their own parking. Thi Lo Su in Umphang is remote and visited by tour with transport included.

faq.q: What hours do Tak's attractions keep?
faq.a: Temples and shrines like the King Taksin Shrine and Wat Thai Watthanaram open through the daytime into late afternoon — go in the morning for smaller crowds and gentler sun. Bhumibol Dam and Lan Sang National Park open during the day. Trok Ban Chin can be walked any time, though the cafés in the old houses run late morning to evening. The Kad Nang Yong Khlong Yam market opens only Saturday–Sunday evenings, roughly 16:00–21:00. Thi Lo Su runs on daytime tour schedules, with the water at its best after the rainy season, roughly November to December. Check hours with each place before setting out.
